title: 3-Read Friday #2: Attention, Y11 Revision, and Landmark Teaching Studies
author: Barton, Craig
summary: In the second issue, Barton curates three posts anchored in the psychology of learning. He leads with Pete Foster's "Attention First," which argues every other teaching technique is wasted if students aren't actually listening, and Barton singles out Foster's opening line as the post's hook. He then welcomes back Dani Quinn from maternity leave with her piece on the pitfalls of sending Year 11 students home with large stacks of printed revision material, a practice Barton clearly recognizes from his own school visits. He closes with InnerDrive's sweep through ten landmark teaching-and-learning studies of the last fifty years, from Miller's 1956 working-memory paper through to 2017 metacognition research, which he calls research "heaven" for a reader like himself. The throughline across all three is evidence-based classroom practice — attention, revision design, and the research base behind them — placing this issue squarely in pedagogy and learning-science territory.
points: Barton treats "all the tasks of the teacher will fail if students aren't listening" as the single most important idea in Foster's post, elevating attention above technique.
He flags printed take-home revision packs as a common but flawed default for Year 11, per Quinn, and notes the lesson applies just as much to Year 10 going forward.
He highlights the InnerDrive studies list as spanning from Miller's 1956 working-memory research to Chen's 2017 metacognition work, using it as a spine for evidence-informed practice.
quotes: I’m obsessed with student attention in lessons, and Pete Foster’s post had me at the first line: All the tasks of the teacher will fail if students aren’t listening.
Pete goes on to share super practical tips to help check and secure student attention throughout a lesson, including when giving instructions and when students are working independently.
Dani returns with a lovely post about the potential pitfalls of a common teacher practice around exam time: giving students loads of printed revision material to take home.
For a research geek like me, this post is heaven. The Inner Drive team reflect on 10 seminal studies that have something important to say about teaching and learning.

We start with Miller’s 1956 study about the limits of working memory that laid the foundations for Cognitive Load Theory, and travel through time to Chen’s 2017 research into metacognition, calling in on studies about forgetting, resilience and mobile phones along the way.
